title: Fill the missing pieces of a persist + flush + refind sequence
description: A working example from Lesson 3: create one book, persist it, flush, then refetch it and assert the Identity Map handed back the same instance. Fill the three blanks.
modelAnswer: em.persist(book) registers the new entity (state: New -> Managed). em.flush() collects all managed changes and writes them in one transaction. After flush, findOne by the same PK returns the same in-memory instance, so book === again is true — proving the Identity Map handed back the canonical reference instead of constructing a fresh object.

title: Predict the query log of a double findOne
description: Predict exactly what the MikroORM debug log prints for this script: persist a Book, flush, then call em.findOne(Book, 1n) twice in a row. How many SELECTs will fire, and what does that prove about the Identity Map?

widgetConfig.prompt: Predict the query log. The EM is freshly forked; debug logging is on.
widgetConfig.command: npm start  # runs: em.persist(book); await em.flush(); await em.findOne(Book, 1n); await em.findOne(Book, 1n);
expectedOutput: // second findOne: no SELECT — instance served from Identity Map

modelAnswer: Expected log: BEGIN, one INSERT, COMMIT, then exactly ONE SELECT for the first findOne. The second findOne fires no SQL — MikroORM checks the Identity Map by PK first, finds the managed Book instance, and returns it. If you see a second SELECT, your EM was forked or cleared between the two calls.

title: Cursor-based pagination — plan, run, revise (AI-resilient)
description:
Implement cursor-based pagination and ship it as a PR. Add 20 articles to your seed. Use em.findByCursor(Article, { first: 5, orderBy: { id: 'desc' } }) for page 1, then pass after: page.endCursor for page 2.

In the PR description, include three things: (1) a short up-front plan — the SQL you expected findByCursor to generate, what the opaque cursor encodes, and what happens to the cursor if you change orderBy mid-session; (2) the actual cursor string (copy-paste) and the real SQL from the query log; (3) a 3-5 sentence revision note comparing plan vs reality — what you got wrong and what you'd change. Also note, in one sentence, what cursor pagination solves that OFFSET cannot.

Submit the link to your branch or PR.
modelAnswer: Cursor pagination encodes the last seen sort-key (here, the article id) into an opaque base64 string. The SQL on page 2 is `WHERE id < :endCursor ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 5`. Changing orderBy mid-session invalidates the cursor because the cursor encodes the sort field — switching fields means the cursor points to nothing meaningful. OFFSET pagination breaks under concurrent inserts (rows shift), and forces the DB to scan + skip; cursor pagination is stable and uses the index directly. An AI answer typically explains the concept but skips the cursor-invalidation gotcha and the row-shift bug under inserts.
